newsitem.title: USA: Consumers pay down debts in September.
newsitem.headline: Consumers pay down debts in September.

text.p: Consumers paid down their debts in September instead of adding to them for the first time in more than three years, the Federal Reserve Board said Thursday.
Total consumer instalment credit shrank $2.6 billion in September at a 2.7 percent annual rate -- the first monthly decline since a small $200-million drop at a 0.3 percent rate in May 1993.
"Most consumers are cutting debt voluntarily and tightening credit standards are forcing others into that position," said Oscar Gonzalez, an economist with John Hancock Financial Services in Boston.
Banks have become more cautious about consumer lending, anticipating that a slower-growing economy will mean smaller gains in incomes and a weaker pace of job growth ahead.
The nation's gross domestic product, or GDP, slowed to a 2.2 percent annual rate in the July-Septmeber third quarter from 4.7 percent in the second quarter, the government previously reported.
Slower consumer spending was a principal reason for the third-quarter easing in growth.
The falloff in September consumer credit followed a revised $5 billion increase in August. It was sharply contrary to analysts' forecasts of an increase in consumer credit of about $5.6 billion.

Auto loans decreased $1 billion in September, at a 3.1 percent annual rate, after rising $700 million, at a 2.2 percent annual rate, in August. Automakers had previously reported a drop in unit sales from August.
"This decline is in line with the general slowdown in consumer spending that we saw this summer," said economist Carl Palash of MCMm MoneyWatch Inc. in New York.
"It fits with a picture of moderate economic growth to the end of the year," he said. But he added that he was not forecasting a weak holiday sales season.
The period from Thanksgiving through Christmas is when retailers make the bulk of their annual sales and most analysts anticipate an improved shopping season this year over last year's weak one.
Previously, the Fed said August consumer credit outstanding had risen by $3.3 billion, but it revised that upward.

The only pickup in consumer credit outstanding in September was in revolving, or credit-card debt, which rose $1 billion at a 2.6 percent annual rate. That followed a $2.5 billion August increase at a 6.7 percent annual rate.

Other credit, a broad-based category that includes consumer bank loans for purposes like buying a mobile home or a boat or paying off education bills, fell by $2.6 billion at a 9.1 percent annual rate in September after rising $1.8 billion at a 6.3 percent rate in August, the Fed said.

Earlier Thursday, the American Bankers Association said that its members were becoming more conservative about making consumer loans and might start considering which industries were most likely to be hurt in an economic slowdown when deciding how to set lending policy.
Joel Naroff, chairman of the ABA's Economic Advisory Committee, told reporters that bankers anticipate the economy may grow by only an anaemic 1 to 1-1/2 percent next year.
Before seasonal adjustment, total outstanding consumer credit in September was $1.18 trillion, up from $1.17 trillion in August and up from $1.08 trillion in September 1995.
